title: Why Did the B-36 Need Ten Engines?

shots.text: This is the Convair B-36 Peacemaker,
the largest piston-engine bomber ever built,
and the only mass-produced aircraft with ten engines.
Six propellers turned at the back of its wings.
shots.caption: Six turning, four burning

shots.text: Four jets burned beneath them.
And it never dropped a bomb in anger.
The Peacemaker was built to fly from America to Europe and back
without refueling, carrying the largest bombs in the arsenal,
at altitudes no fighter of its day could reach.
But getting there took a compromise so strange that crews gave
it a slogan: six turning, four burning.
Why would anyone build an airplane with ten engines?
The answer starts with a problem no one had solved before.
It is 1941, and Britain is fighting for its life.
German armies have overrun most of Europe, and American planners are asking
a frightening question. What if Britain falls? The United States would have no air bases close to Germany,
and no bomber in existence could fly from America,
strike a target in Europe, and come home again.
The Army Air Corps wrote down what that bomber would have to do. It would need to carry about 4,500 kilograms of bombs over
10,400 nautical miles without refueling,
at 390 knots, above 45,000 feet.
No aircraft had ever come close to those numbers.
The largest bombers of the day, the B-17 Flying Fortress and
the B-24 Liberator, could manage about half the range with a
fraction of the load. And the physics was brutal.
Range meant fuel, and fuel meant weight.
Weight meant a bigger wing, and a bigger wing meant more drag. More drag meant more power, and more power meant more engines,
which meant still more weight. Every answer made the problem bigger.
The contract went to Consolidated Aircraft of Fort Worth,
Texas, in October 1941,
before America had even entered the war. So let's start with why the B-36 was built.
Consolidated Aircraft, soon renamed Convair, took the contract in
October 1941 and set to work in Fort Worth,
Texas. The design team, led by Ted Hall, started with the wing. Nothing else mattered until the wing was big enough
to lift the fuel, the bombs, and the engines themselves.
It grew to 230 feet across, wider than any wing ever put on
a combat aircraft. The engines came next.
The most powerful piston engine America had was the Pratt and Whitney R-4360
Wasp Major, a 28-cylinder radial that made 3,500
horsepower. Six of them would hang on the trailing edge of the wing,
facing backward, driving pusher propellers. The arrangement kept the wing clean, but it starved the engines of cooling
air, and overheating would haunt the bomber for its whole career. The prototype, the XB-36, rolled out in August 1945,
just as the war ended, and it first flew on 8 August 1946,
with test pilots Beryl Erickson and G.
S. Green at the controls, from Carswell Air Force Base
in Fort Worth. The first version stood on single huge main
wheels that sank into soft runways, so production aircraft got
four-wheel bogies instead. The Air Force accepted its first B-36A
in June 1948, and the 7th Bombardment Wing at Carswell became the first unit to fly it.
By then the war the bomber was designed for was over, and a new one, the Cold War, had already begun.
The version we're looking at is the B-36D, the first version with all
ten engines, and the variant that entered service in 1949.
It is 49.4 meters long, 14.25 meters
tall, and its wingspan is 70.1 meters.
That wing is longer than a Boeing B-52's by almost 14 meters,

overlays.text: Almost 14 m longer than a B-52

shots.text: and it remains the longest wing ever put on a combat aircraft.

overlays.text: Longest wing of any combat aircraft

shots.text: The bomber could climb to 45,200 feet,
cruise at 200 knots, and reach 381 knots with every engine
running. Its range was 6,500 nautical miles with a full
bomb load, and 8,700 nautical miles with a light one,
far enough to cross an ocean and come back.
It could carry 39,000 kilograms of bombs,
more than ten times the load of a B-17,
with a crew of 15. Now,
let's take a closer look at how the aircraft is laid out.
Up front is the glazed nose, where the bombardier sat,
with the pressurized flight deck above and behind it.
The fuselage is deep and round, finished in bare metal,
and it holds two pressurized compartments.
The crew moved between them through a tunnel 26 meters long on a small
wheeled trolley, past a galley and six bunks for rest on missions that
could last 40 hours. Moving toward the middle of the aircraft,
we have the wing, running straight through the fuselage,
and the four bomb bays beneath it.
The wing is so thick at the root that a man could crawl inside it to work on the fuel
system. Behind the wing, on its trailing edge,
sit the six piston engines, mounted backward.
Each one is a Pratt and Whitney R-4360 Wasp Major,
a 28-cylinder radial making 3,500 horsepower,
and each one turns a three-bladed propeller 5.8 meters across.
The propellers sit behind the wing, pushing the bomber forward instead of pulling it,
and their slow beat made a low pulse on the ground that gave the bomber away long
before it arrived. The main landing gear stands on four-wheel bogies,
built to spread a weight of about 162,000 kilograms across the
runway. At the tail is a single tall fin,
and below it, in the tail cone, sat the rear gunner,
alone. Then came the strangest feature of all.
Under each outer wing hangs a pod, and each pod holds two General
Electric J47 turbojets.
That is four jets, each making 5,200 pounds of thrust,
bolted onto an airplane that already had six piston engines.
With all ten running, the bomber had about 40,000 horsepower for short bursts.
But the jets were not for cruising. They drank fuel so fast that the crew used
them only for takeoff, for climbing, and for a fast dash over the target.
Then the crew shut them down and closed the louvers over the pods to cut drag.
Six engines carried the bomber across the ocean.
Four more got it off the ground and over the target.
That was the deal.
Now, let's go back to how the B-36 was used. It became the backbone of Strategic Air Command,
under General Curtis LeMay, and the only bomber that could carry the nuclear
weapons of the day across an ocean. That role made it the center of the fiercest
budget fight in American military history.
In April 1949, the Navy laid the keel of a 65,000-ton
supercarrier, the USS United States,
built to launch nuclear bombers from the sea. Five days later,
Secretary of Defense Louis Johnson cancelled it and sent the money to the B-36
instead. The Secretary of the Navy resigned in protest,
and the admirals took their case to Congress, calling the bomber a billion-dollar
blunder. The hearings ran through October 1949,
and the Chief of Naval Operations, Admiral Louis Denfeld,
lost his job for speaking against the decision.
The Air Force won the argument, and the B-36 stayed.
More than a third of all B-36s were built as RB-36 reconnaissance
aircraft, carrying a crew of 22 and up to 23 cameras.
From 1951 they probed the edges of the Soviet Arctic,
flying from England and Japan at altitudes no fighter of the day could
reach. The bomber also had its disasters.
On 13 February 1950, a B-36B
flying a simulated strike from Alaska ran into trouble when three of its engines
caught fire. The crew jettisoned its Mark 4 bomb over the Pacific,
where it detonated, and bailed out over the coast of British Columbia.
Twelve of the 17 men survived. Five were lost, including the weaponeer, Captain Theodore Schreier.
The empty bomber flew on for about 200 miles and crashed into
Mount Kologet. It was the first time America had ever lost a nuclear
weapon. In 1954, the Air Force stripped the
guns and armor from the surviving bombers in the Featherweight program,
trading protection for altitude. But the jet age was already here.
The B-47 and the B-52 were faster, and the B-36, designed before the war,
was running out of time.
The last B-36 in service retired on 12 February 1959,
after ten years with Strategic Air Command.
The last flight of all came two months later,
when a B-36J flew from its desert storage in Arizona to
the National Museum of the United States Air Force in Dayton,
Ohio. Most of the fleet was cut up for scrap at Davis-Monthan
Air Force Base. Four complete aircraft survive.
One stands in Dayton, one in Tucson, Arizona,
one in Ashland, Nebraska, and one in Atwater,
California, the only reconnaissance version left.
The B-36 never flew in combat.
It never dropped a bomb in anger. It spent its whole career waiting
for a war that never came.
So here is why the B-36 needed ten engines.
Because the mission demanded a weight no six engines could lift at the speed the
jet age required. The range demanded fuel,
and the fuel demanded a wing 230 feet across,
and the wing demanded power. Six piston engines gave the
bomber its endurance. They could carry it across an ocean and keep it
there for 40 hours. But they could not get that weight off the ground quickly,
they could not climb it fast, and they could not push it over a defended target
at 381 knots. Four jets could do all three,
for a few minutes at a time. It was not elegance.
It was arithmetic. Six engines for the long cruise,
four engines for the hard moments, and a slogan that told the whole story.
Six turning, four burning.
The B-36 held the line for ten years, until a bomber arrived that did
the same job with eight jets and no propellers at all.
The Boeing B-52 Stratofortress replaced it,
and then it did something the B-36 never managed.
It stayed. Find out why by watching our video on the Boeing B-52 Stratofortress now.
